author: A Robot
objectives: Represent a two-dimensional vector by its magnitude and direction, and equivalently by its horizontal and vertical components.
Add two or more vectors graphically using the tip-to-tail method and identify the resultant vector.
Decompose a vector into components along the x- and y-axes using right-triangle trigonometry, and reconstruct the original vector from its components.
Explain why the horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile are independent of one another, given that gravity acts only in the vertical direction.

Describe how the horizontal velocity, vertical velocity, and position of a projectile change over the course of its flight, and identify the moment of maximum height as the point where the vertical velocity is zero.

Predict how changes in initial launch angle and launch speed affect the trajectory, range, and maximum height of a projectile, and identify the launch angle that produces maximum range for a given speed.

modules.description: This module explores vectors as mathematical objects, focusing on their representation by magnitude and direction, decomposition into components, and graphical addition.
modules.author: A Robot

Decompose a vector into components along the x- and y-axes using right-triangle trigonometry, and reconstruct the original vector from its components.

clips.narration: Vectors are fundamental in physics for quantities possessing both magnitude and direction. We'll start by visualizing a single vector.

clips.changeMeaning: Show a vector with its components.
clips.narration: A vector can be represented by its magnitude and direction, or by its components along the x and y axes. Here's a vector and its components.

clips.changeMeaning: Demonstrate vector addition using the tip-to-tail method.
clips.narration: Vectors can be added graphically. By placing the tail of one vector at the tip of another, we find the resultant vector.

clips.changeMeaning: Show vector decomposition into x and y components.
clips.narration: We can also decompose a vector into its horizontal (x) and vertical (y) components using trigonometry.

modules.description: This module applies vector operations to understand the physics of projectile motion, examining the independence of horizontal and vertical motion and the effect of initial conditions.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain why the horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile are independent of one another, given that gravity acts only in the vertical direction.

Describe how the horizontal velocity, vertical velocity, and position of a projectile change over the course of its flight, and identify the moment of maximum height as the point where the vertical velocity is zero.

Predict how changes in initial launch angle and launch speed affect the trajectory, range, and maximum height of a projectile, and identify the launch angle that produces maximum range for a given speed.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduce projectile motion and its initial velocity vector.
clips.narration: Now let's apply these vector concepts to projectile motion. The initial velocity of a projectile can be decomposed into horizontal and vertical components.

clips.changeMeaning: Demonstrate the independence of horizontal and vertical motion.
clips.narration: Crucially, the horizontal and vertical motions are independent. Gravity only affects the vertical motion, while the horizontal velocity remains constant.

clips.changeMeaning: Show the parabolic trajectory resulting from combined motions.
clips.narration: The combination of constant horizontal velocity and uniformly accelerated vertical motion results in a parabolic trajectory.

clips.changeMeaning: Illustrate how changing launch angle and speed affects trajectory, range, and height.
clips.narration: Changing the initial launch angle and speed will alter the projectile's trajectory, maximum height, and range. Observe how these parameters influence the flight.

clips.changeMeaning: Identify the launch angle for maximum range.
clips.narration: For a given launch speed, a launch angle of 45 degrees typically results in the maximum horizontal range. This is a key outcome of projectile motion analysis.
